learn.title: Floating Offshore Wind Platforms Explained
learn.intro: Floating offshore wind unlocks vast clean energy potential in deep waters beyond traditional fixed-foundation turbines. As nations seek to decarbonize electricity grids, these advanced platforms enable access to stronger, more consistent winds far from shore, accelerating the global shift toward renewable energy systems.
learn.c1_text: Floating platforms come in three main types: spar, semi-submersible, and tension-leg. Each design balances stability, cost, and ease of deployment. These structures typically rise over 100 meters above sea level and can capture winds exceeding 25 m/s, offering massive energy yields compared to onshore sites.
learn.c3_text: India has identified over 300 GW potential in offshore wind, including deep-water zones ideal for floating tech. The National Institute of Ocean Technology is piloting floating projects off Tamil Nadu. With supportive policies, India could become a leader in Asia’s emerging floating wind market.
learn.stat2: Average offshore wind speed: 8–10 m/s vs. 4–6 m/s onshore
learn.stat4: Floating turbine capacity: up to 15 MW per unit

learn.title: Geothermal Energy: Tapping Earth's Core Power
learn.intro: Geothermal energy taps into the Earth’s internal heat to produce clean, reliable baseload power and direct-use applications. Unlike solar or wind, it operates continuously, making it a cornerstone technology for stable, low-carbon energy systems worldwide.
learn.c1_text: The Earth’s core generates immense heat—about 44 trillion watts flow through the planet’s crust daily. Geothermal plants tap underground reservoirs where water or steam rises naturally, driving turbines much like a kettle boiling water—but powered by magma miles beneath our feet.
learn.c2_text: Three main geothermal plant types exist: dry steam, flash steam, and binary cycle. Flash plants dominate globally, using high-pressure hot water (above 182°C) to spin turbines. Binary systems use lower temps (100–180°C), expanding hot fluid to drive generators indirectly.
learn.c3_text: India ranks 5th globally in geothermal potential, especially in the Himalayan foothills and western regions. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy targets 1 GW by 2030. Pilot projects in Ladakh and Assam aim to harness thermal gradients for remote power needs.
learn.stat2: Geothermal provides 24/7 baseload power at 90% uptime
learn.stat3: India's geothermal potential: 10 GW across 340 sites
learn.stat4: Binary cycle plants operate at 10–180°C resource range

learn.title: Wind Turbine Lifespan & Blade Recycling
learn.intro: Wind turbines last 20–25 years, but managing end-of-life blades remains a key challenge. Recycling old components ensures sustainability and supports circular economy goals as the wind industry scales globally to meet net-zero targets.
learn.c1_text: Modern wind turbines are designed for 20–25 years of operation under harsh conditions—hurricane-force winds, temperature swings, and constant vibration. Regular maintenance, including gearbox checks and blade inspections, extends performance and prevents costly downtime.
learn.c2_text: Most blades are made of fiberglass-reinforced composites, hard to recycle. Methods include mechanical shredding, chemical decomposition, and repurposing into cement feedstock. Emerging techniques recover carbon fibers and reuse materials in new products or construction.
learn.c3_text: India has over 40 GW of wind capacity, with many turbines nearing retirement. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy is developing policies for blade disposal. Startups like ReBlade are exploring recycling solutions tailored to Indian climates and infrastructure.
learn.stat4: 720,000 tons of blade waste expected annually by 2050

learn.title: Agrivoltaics: Solar Panels Meet Farming
learn.intro: Agrivoltaics combines solar panel installations with agricultural land use, increasing both food and energy output. This innovative approach addresses land-use conflicts while boosting farm resilience and renewable energy adoption.
learn.c1_text: By installing solar panels above crops or grazing areas, farms generate income from two sources simultaneously. Panels reduce soil evaporation and protect plants from extreme weather, while elevated structures allow continued farming underneath—a win-win for farmers and energy producers.
learn.c2_text: Studies show certain crops grow better under partial shade, reducing heat stress and water needs. Leafy greens, tomatoes, and herbs often thrive. Meanwhile, solar panels operate more efficiently when cooled by transpiration from plants below, boosting overall system productivity.
learn.c3_text: India's National Solar Mission promotes agri-PV models. States like Gujarat and Rajasthan pilot dual-use farms. The World Bank supports $1 billion in financing for such projects, aiming to add 30 GW of solar capacity without displacing agriculture or forests.
learn.stat1: Agrivoltaic yields increase by 60% in some crop studies
learn.stat2: Solar panel efficiency gains: +2–5% with cooling
learn.stat3: India targets 280 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030
learn.stat4: Dual-use farms reduce water usage by up to 20%

learn.title: Bifacial Solar Panels: Power From Both Sides
learn.intro: Bifacial solar panels capture sunlight from both front and back surfaces, increasing energy yield by up to 30%. Their growing adoption enhances solar farm economics and supports higher returns on investment in utility-scale installations.
learn.c1_text: Traditional panels only absorb light on one side. Bifacial modules use transparent backsheets or glass-glass construction to collect reflected light from the ground or snow. This boosts output during early morning and late afternoon hours when direct sunlight is limited.
learn.c2_text: To maximize bifacial gains, panels must be elevated (1–2 meters) and installed over reflective surfaces like white gravel or snow. Tracking systems that follow the sun further enhance energy capture, especially in open fields with minimal shading.
learn.c3_text: India’s Bhadla Solar Park—one of the world’s largest—uses bifacial panels to achieve record-low tariffs. Domestic manufacturers like Tata Power Solar are ramping up production. Government tenders increasingly specify bifacial modules for large projects.
learn.stat1: Bifacial panels increase yield by 5–30% depending on albedo
learn.stat3: Bifacial module cost premium: ~10–20% over monofacial

learn.title: Solar Inverters: String, Micro, and Hybrid Explained
learn.intro: Solar inverters convert DC power from panels into usable AC electricity for homes and grids. Choosing the right type impacts system efficiency, cost, and reliability—making this often-overlooked component critical to successful solar installations.
learn.c1_text: These central inverters connect multiple panels in series, converting DC to AC at one point. They’re cost-effective and widely used in residential and commercial systems. However, if one panel is shaded, it can drag down the entire string’s performance.
learn.c2_text: Microinverters attach to each panel, optimizing individual output—ideal for shaded roofs. Hybrid inverters work with battery storage, managing both solar input and grid interaction. They offer flexibility but come at a higher upfront cost than standard string units.
learn.c3_text: India’s solar auctions increasingly require string inverters with anti-PID and remote monitoring features. Domestic companies like ABB India and Delta Electronics supply hybrid inverters compatible with lithium-ion batteries, supporting the government’s storage-focused policies.
learn.stat1: String inverters account for 80% of global solar installations
learn.stat2: Microinverters improve system efficiency by 5–25% in shaded conditions
learn.stat3: India’s solar inverter demand: 15 GW annually (2024)
learn.stat4: Hybrid inverters integrate with batteries at 98% round-trip efficiency
